summary:
FireBridge is a free website that turns 25 years of NASA satellite fire detections into one consistent fire history for any area you pick on a map.

The challenge is that the record is split. MODIS has tracked fires since 2001 and is retiring. Its successor, VIIRS, counts 5 to 9 times more hotspots for the same fires, so joining the two makes fire seem to explode in 2012. FireBridge fixes that. It learns how the two sensors match during the years they flew together (2012 to 2018), separately for each region and land type, then translates VIIRS onto the MODIS scale. On years it never saw, the result lands within 1% of MODIS.

From that one record, FireBridge builds a burning activity calendar for any area: the usual fire season, the worst years, this month versus normal, and how the latest fire ranks against every fire since 2001. Live NASA FIRMS data updates it every hour, and every hotspot can be downloaded.

That matters because fire agencies need to know whether this season is unusual. Without harmonization, they lose their 25-year baseline as MODIS shuts down.
details:
FireBridge is a free website that shows when and where fires have burned, from 2001 to today. Draw an area on a map (or type coordinates, or search for a town), pick your dates, and FireBridge gives you a burning activity calendar of every month since 2001. It shows the area’s usual fire season, its highest-risk months, how this month compares with the 2003-2022 normal, and how the latest fire ranks against every fire there since 2001. A map replays the fire season month by month, and everything downloads as CSV, GeoJSON or KML.

How it works:

The record comes from two satellite instruments. MODIS (on Terra and Aqua, since 2001) is retiring. Its successor, VIIRS (since 2012), has sharper pixels and reports 5 to 9 times more hotspots for the same fires. If you join the two records as they are, fire seems to explode in 2012. That jump is fake.

From 2012 to 2018, MODIS Aqua and VIIRS S-NPP flew almost the same orbit, so we use those years to learn how the two instruments relate. The method is quantile mapping, fitted separately for each region, each land-cover type (from NASA’s MODIS land cover product) and day or night. Then we translate every VIIRS detection onto the MODIS scale.

We tested it on years the method never saw (2019 onward). The harmonized record lands within 1% of MODIS overall, while raw VIIRS is off by 660%. On NOAA-20, a satellite we never used for fitting, it lands within 3%. An independent check against NASA’s MODIS burned-area product shows the 2012 jump is gone. A live NASA FIRMS feed updates the current month every hour. Gas flares and other fixed heat sources are filtered out, and days with no satellite data show up as missing, not as zero fire.

Benefits and impact:

As MODIS retires, fire agencies risk losing their 25-year baseline. FireBridge keeps it. An emergency manager can see in seconds whether this month is unusual. A land manager can plan around the real fire season. A scientist can study trends without a fake jump in 2012. An “unusual right now” list points to the places furthest above normal this month, for early warning.

Creativity:

The usual shortcut is one global ratio between the two sensors. We match them per region and per land type instead. In two of our three test regions, that cuts the error roughly in half (in the Amazon, one ratio does slightly better). We also group hotspots into fire clusters so a new fire can be ranked against every past fire, not just past months. The site is map-first like a weather app, explains every number in plain language, since the challenge comes from Argentina’s space agency, CONAE.

Tools:

Python (pandas, NumPy, SciPy, DuckDB over Parquet, rasterio) runs the pipeline and statistics. FastAPI serves the data. The website is plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with Leaflet for the map and D3 and Chart.js for the charts. It runs in Docker on Azure Container Apps, with data on Hugging Face. GitHub Actions runs our tests on every push, and Playwright checks every feature in a real browser. No special hardware was needed: just laptops and free cloud tiers. We used Claude Code as a coding assistant, and our team reviewed and ran everything.

Factors we considered:

Scientific honesty came first. We tested on held-out years and on a satellite we never fitted to, and we publish where the method struggles. Texas runs about 6% high, and MODIS itself drifts in orbit after 2022. A fit from one region also does not carry over to another, so each new region needs its own fit, which is doable worldwide because the 2012-2018 overlap exists everywhere.

Accessibility mattered: colorblind-safe colors, screen-reader data tables, keyboard navigation and phone layouts.

For everyday use, we added shareable links, a one-page printable briefing and standard GIS file formats.

For reliability, we pinned every library version and the dataset version. 133 automated checks confirm that every number on the site matches the data.
